title: 1 Chronicles 6:1–15
context: 1 Chronicles 6 is devoted to the tribe of Levi. In English Bibles and the WEB, 6:1–15 corresponds to Hebrew 5:27–41, and 6:16–81 corresponds to Hebrew 6:1–66; the WEB numbering is kept here. The first unit, 6:1–15, traces the line of high priests from Levi through Aaron and Eleazar to Jehozadak, who went into exile when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem away by Nebuchadnezzar. The list runs through Zadok, the priest of David’s and Solomon’s time, and Hilkiah, the priest of Josiah’s reform (2 Kings 22). It does not include every priest named elsewhere, such as Jehoiada (2 Kings 11), and it omits Eli’s family of Ithamar; Ezra 7:1–5 gives a shorter form of this line. Chronicles does not explain these selections, and these notes do not attempt to harmonize the lists. Arminian and Reformed readers share the main reading: God kept a faithful priestly line through Israel’s history, through the exile and beyond, so that atonement and worship could continue.

verses.text: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
verses.arminianNotes: Levi’s three sons, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, head the chapter as in Exodus 6:16 and Numbers 3:17. Arminian readers see God setting apart a whole tribe for his service, a calling the Levites were to answer with faithful lives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s choice of Levi for sanctuary service as an act of his grace. Both traditions read the opening as rooting Israel’s worship in the families God appointed, which is shared ground.

verses.text: The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.
verses.arminianNotes: Kohath’s four sons are Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, matching Exodus 6:18. Arminians note that the Kohathite line will produce both the priests and many Levites who serve at the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the list preparing to trace the priestly line through Amram. Both traditions treat the verse as a simple genealogical link without theological dispute.

verses.text: The children of Amram: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
verses.arminianNotes: Amram’s children are Aaron, Moses, and Miriam, and Aaron’s sons are Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Arminian readers recall that Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire (Leviticus 10:1–2), a sober warning about approaching God carelessly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the line continues through Eleazar. Both traditions see the mention of Miriam alongside Moses and Aaron as honoring her place in the exodus story, and they share the reading of Nadab and Abihu’s judgment.

verses.text: Eleazar became the father of Phinehas, Phinehas became the father of Abishua,
verses.arminianNotes: Eleazar became the father of Phinehas, who became the father of Abishua. Arminians recall Phinehas’s zeal in Numbers 25, where God gave him a covenant of lasting priesthood in response to his faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the covenant with Phinehas as God’s gracious promise to preserve this priestly line. Both traditions read the verse as the start of a line God kept through many generations.

verses.text: Abishua became the father of Bukki. Bukki became the father of Uzzi.
verses.arminianNotes: Abishua became the father of Bukki, and Bukki of Uzzi. Arminian readers note that most of these priests are otherwise unknown, yet their names are preserved, showing that God remembers faithful service even when history records little about it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence in maintaining the line through ordinary generations. Both traditions read these names as a quiet testimony to God’s steady care for his worship.

verses.text: Uzzi became the father of Zerahiah. Zerahiah became the father of Meraioth.
verses.arminianNotes: Uzzi became the father of Zerahiah, and Zerahiah of Meraioth. Arminians see the genealogy continuing generation by generation, each priest receiving and passing on the calling God gave to Aaron’s family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress God’s faithfulness in keeping the priesthood alive. Both traditions treat these verses as shared ground and avoid building speculation on names the text does not explain.

verses.text: Meraioth became the father of Amariah. Amariah became the father of Ahitub.
verses.arminianNotes: Meraioth became the father of Amariah, and Amariah of Ahitub. Arminian readers note that the names Amariah and Ahitub appear again later in the list (6:11), which shows that families often reused names across generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the repeated names make the list harder to follow but do not change its purpose. Both traditions read the verse as part of a carefully kept record of the priestly line.

verses.text: Ahitub became the father of Zadok. Zadok became the father of Ahimaaz.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahitub became the father of Zadok, and Zadok of Ahimaaz. Zadok is the priest of David’s and Solomon’s time (2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Kings 2:35). Arminians see God raising up a faithful priest to serve in a critical period.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Zadok’s line replaced Eli’s family, as foretold in 1 Samuel 2:27–36 and recorded in 1 Kings 2:27. Both traditions see God’s word being fulfilled through the priestly succession.

verses.text: Ahimaaz became the father of Azariah. Azariah became the father of Johanan.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimaaz became the father of Azariah, and Azariah of Johanan. Arminian readers recall Ahimaaz as the runner who brought news to David (2 Samuel 18), a reminder that the people in these lists lived real lives in Israel’s history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. An Azariah son of Zadok is named among Solomon’s officials in 1 Kings 4:2, and interpreters discuss how he relates to this list. Both traditions avoid forcing a resolution where the text does not give one.

verses.text: Johanan became the father of Azariah, who executed the priest’s office in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Johanan became the father of Azariah, who served as priest in the temple Solomon built. Arminians see the temple as the place where this priestly line carried out its calling for generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Interpreters discuss whether the note about serving in Solomon’s temple belongs to this Azariah or to the Azariah of 6:9, who lived in Solomon’s time. Both traditions leave the question open rather than harmonizing it.

verses.text: Azariah became the father of Amariah. Amariah became the father of Ahitub.
verses.arminianNotes: Azariah became the father of Amariah, and Amariah of Ahitub. Arminian readers note that an Amariah served as chief priest under Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 19:11), though the text does not say whether he is the same man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and hedge any identification. Both traditions see the list continuing God’s provision of priests through the period of the kings, without claiming certainty about every name.

verses.text: Ahitub became the father of Zadok. Zadok became the father of Shallum.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahitub became the father of Zadok, and Zadok of Shallum. Arminians note that the names Ahitub and Zadok recur here, another sign that families honored earlier ancestors by reusing names.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the repetition as part of the family’s memory of God’s faithfulness to Zadok’s line. Both traditions treat the verse as a simple genealogical link.

verses.text: Shallum became the father of Hilkiah. Hilkiah became the father of Azariah.
verses.arminianNotes: Shallum became the father of Hilkiah, and Hilkiah of Azariah. Hilkiah is the priest who found the book of the law in Josiah’s day (2 Kings 22:8). Arminian readers see a faithful priest whose discovery led to repentance and reform.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence in bringing his word back to light through Hilkiah. Both traditions read the reference as a reminder that the priestly line played a key role in Israel’s renewal.

verses.text: Azariah became the father of Seraiah. Seraiah became the father of Jehozadak.
verses.arminianNotes: Azariah became the father of Seraiah, and Seraiah of Jehozadak. Seraiah was the chief priest executed after Jerusalem fell (2 Kings 25:18–21). Arminians see the cost of judgment falling even on the priestly family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Jehozadak’s son Joshua became high priest after the return (Haggai 1:1). Both traditions see God preserving the line through judgment so that worship could resume.

verses.text: Jehozadak went into captivity when the LORD carried Judah and Jerusalem away by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehozadak went into captivity when the LORD carried Judah and Jerusalem away by Nebuchadnezzar. Arminian readers see the exile as God’s judgment for persistent unfaithfulness, carried out through a foreign king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the text names the LORD as the one who carried Judah away. Both traditions read the verse as showing God’s rule over the exile and his faithfulness in preserving the priestly line through it.
